title: What Are We Buying When We Buy an AI Tutor?
author: Nick Potkalitsky, Ph.D.
summary: Nick Potkalitsky, Ph.D., asks what educational institutions are actually purchasing when they buy an AI tutoring platform—and argues the answer is not instruction, but delivery capacity. Drawing on several years of emerging evidence, he reviews the two strongest positive results: Gregory Kestin's Harvard RCT, where a custom AI tutor doubled physics learning gains in less time, and the World Bank's Nigeria study, where Microsoft Copilot added 0.23 SD in English scores over six weeks with teacher mediation. In both cases, however, Potkalitsky shows that the gains came from tightly controlled instructional conditions (scaffolded practice, teacher oversight, assessment alignment)—not from the AI environment itself. Khan Academy's own acknowledgment that Khanmigo's early results were more modest than hoped reinforces the point: engagement and perceived helpfulness can rise without producing a distinctive learning effect. Potkalitsky applies Richard Clark's 1983 'media as vehicle' argument to show that AI tutoring research follows the same pattern as earlier educational technology research: the instructional method does the work, not the medium. He also identifies a Matthew effect—students with higher baseline performance and stronger metacognitive habits benefit most, contradicting the sales pitch that AI tutoring automatically helps the students furthest behind. The purchasing question, Potkalitsky concludes, should shift from 'does AI tutoring work in the abstract?' to 'what instructional method does this environment enforce, and do gains transfer beyond the platform's own tasks?'
points: The strongest positive AI tutoring results (Harvard physics, World Bank Nigeria) emerged from carefully engineered instructional conditions—scaffolded practice, teacher mediation, close assessment alignment—not from the AI environment itself, meaning districts purchasing 'AI interactive spaces' may be buying delivery capacity without the instruction that made those environments work.

Richard Clark's 1983 'media as vehicle' argument holds: researchers and administrators often confuse the medium (an AI platform) with the instructional method packaged inside it, and the older intelligent tutoring systems literature confirms that effect sizes shrink substantially when measurement shifts from purpose-built assessments to standardised tests.

AI tutoring exhibits a Matthew effect—students with higher baseline knowledge, stronger metacognitive habits, and existing comfort with self-paced abstract study benefit most—which directly contradicts the promotional claim that AI tutoring automatically rescues the students furthest behind.

Khanmigo's early results are instructive: students liked it and found it helpful, but controlled studies found no statistically significant advantage over Google search or paper—demonstrating that perceived usefulness and actual learning effects can diverge significantly.

The purchasing question should shift from 'is this AI environment effective in the abstract?' to 'what instructional method does this environment enforce, what evidence supports that method, which students benefit, and do gains transfer beyond the platform's own practice tasks?'
quotes: Districts and universities are buying into these systems on the premise that the space itself is the instructional advance, as if placing students inside an AI-mediated environment will reliably produce better learning.

The strongest studies, however, do not show that an interactive AI environment works by itself. They show that carefully designed scaffolding, close alignment between practice and assessment, supplemental time, and teacher mediation can produce gains when AI is one part of the instructional arrangement.

Kestin’s tutor was not a general-purpose chatbot dropped into a physics course. It had the correct solutions in advance, released help one step at a time, required students to attempt work before receiving explanations, and targeted the same material measured by researcher-built pre- and post-tests.

Students liked Khanmigo and saw it as a helpful supplement, but the quantitative result did not show that the AI tutor outperformed the alternatives. That is exactly the pattern districts should care about: engagement and perceived helpfulness can rise without producing a distinctive learning effect.
His claim was not that technology is irrelevant. It was that researchers often confuse the medium with the instructional method delivered through it.

Students who already know how to ask questions, persist through confusion, interpret feedback, and connect examples to underlying concepts are better prepared to benefit from an AI tutor. Students without those habits may need more human structure, not less.

The truck is still not the groceries. Institutions buying AI tutoring environments are buying delivery capacity, and delivery capacity can matter. The hard question is whether the system contains instruction worth delivering.
